items.stem: In which state do particles have the most energy?
items.answer: Gas
items.markingKey: C. Fastest movement.

items.stem: "Particles expand when a substance is heated." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The particles stay the same size; they move faster and further apart, so the substance expands.
items.markingKey: The particles stay the same size; they move faster and further apart, so the substance expands. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a liquid and a gas.
items.answer: In a liquid particles are close together and slide past each other, so it has a fixed volume; in a gas particles are far apart and move freely, so it fills any volume.
items.markingKey: In a liquid particles are close together and slide past each other, so it has a fixed volume; in a gas particles are far apart and move freely, so it fills any volume. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Brownian motion (1827) as an example, explain evidence for moving particles.
items.answer: Robert Brown saw pollen grains in water jiggling randomly under a microscope; in 1905 Einstein explained this as water molecules bombarding the grains. It gave strong evidence that atoms and molecules exist and are constantly moving.
items.markingKey: Context (Robert Brown saw pollen grains in water jiggling randomly under a microscope; in 1905 Einstein explained this as water molecules bombarding the grains.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It gave strong evidence that atoms and molecules exist and are constantly moving. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evidence for moving particles.

items.stem: Arjun wants to find out how the temperature of a gas in a sealed syringe affects its volume. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does temperature of the water bath around the syringe affect volume of air in the syringe?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (temperature of the water bath around the syringe (°C)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (volume of air in the syringe read from the scale) in a question form.

items.stem:
Noah heated a sealed flask of air and measured the pressure inside with a pressure sensor (three runs).

Temperature / °C | Pressure / kPa: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 101 | 101 | 96
20 | 108 | 106 | 105
40 | 114 | 117 | 111
60 | 118 | 119 | 157
80 | 128 | 125 | 129

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean pressure at 60 °C, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 157 kPa (trial 3 at 60 °C); mean = 118.5 kPa
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (157) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 118.5 kPa.

items.stem: Maya plans an investigation into how the temperature of a gas in a sealed syringe affects its volume. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (temperature of the water bath around the syringe (°C)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Draw (describe) and compare the arrangement, movement and forces between particles in ice, water and steam, and use these to explain one property of each.
items.answer: Ice: regular, close-packed, vibrate, strong forces – fixed shape. Water: close, random, slide past each other, weaker forces – flows, takes container shape but fixed volume. Steam: far apart, random, fast in all directions, negligible forces – fills container, can be compressed.
items.markingKey: Ice: regular, close-packed, vibrate, strong forces – fixed shape. Water: close, random, slide past each other, weaker forces – flows, takes container shape but fixed volume. Steam: far apart, random, fast in all directions, negligible forces – fills container, can be compressed.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The idea that all matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving"?
items.answer: particle model
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of particle model.

items.stem: Explain, using the particle model, why solids have a fixed shape.
items.answer: Particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces of attraction; they can only vibrate, so the shape does not change.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces of attraction; they can only vibrate, so the shape does not change. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Particles in a solid do not move." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions; they move faster as the solid is heated.
items.markingKey: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions; they move faster as the solid is heated. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Mateo heated a sealed flask of air and measured the pressure inside with a pressure sensor (three runs).

Temperature / °C | Pressure / kPa: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 93 | 93 | 91
20 | 96 | 96 | 96
40 | 102 | 106 | 105
60 | 114 | 114 | 110
80 | 114 | 115 | 118

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The pressure increases steadily as temperature increases. At higher temperature gas particles move faster, so they collide with the walls more often and with more force, increasing pressure.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The pressure increases steadily as temperature increases.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: At higher temperature gas particles move faster, so they collide with the walls more often and with more force, increasing pressure.

items.stem: Leila is investigating how the temperature of a gas in a sealed syringe affects its volume. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If the temperature increases, then the volume of the gas will increase, because the particles move faster and push the plunger out further.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If the temperature increases, then the volume of the gas will increase, because the particles move faster and push the plunger out further.

items.stem: Briefly describe Brownian motion (1827) and explain what it reveals about evidence for moving particles.
items.answer: Robert Brown saw pollen grains in water jiggling randomly under a microscope; in 1905 Einstein explained this as water molecules bombarding the grains. It gave strong evidence that atoms and molecules exist and are constantly moving.
items.markingKey: Context (Robert Brown saw pollen grains in water jiggling randomly under a microscope; in 1905 Einstein explained this as water molecules bombarding the grains.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It gave strong evidence that atoms and molecules exist and are constantly moving. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evidence for moving particles.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Scientists should replace the solid–liquid–gas model with a more complicated one in school science."
items.answer: The three-state particle model is a good starting point; its limits should be discussed as students meet substances it cannot explain.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: real substances include plasmas, gels and glasses that do not fit neatly. Arguments against: the simple model explains most everyday observations; more complex models are hard to understand without the basics first. Supported judgement: The three-state particle model is a good starting point; its limits should be discussed as students meet substances it cannot explain. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which substance sublimes at room temperature?
items.answer: Solid carbon dioxide (dry ice)
items.markingKey: D. It turns straight to gas.

items.stem: Briefly explain why water condenses on the outside of a cold can of drink.
items.answer: Water vapour in the air touches the cold surface, loses energy and condenses into droplets.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Water vapour in the air touches the cold surface, loses energy and condenses into droplets. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Steam is the white cloud you see above a kettle." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Steam is invisible water vapour; the white cloud is tiny droplets that have already condensed.
items.markingKey: Steam is invisible water vapour; the white cloud is tiny droplets that have already condensed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Sana is investigating how the surface area of water affects the rate of evaporation. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If the surface area is larger, then more water will evaporate, because more particles are at the surface where they can escape.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If the surface area is larger, then more water will evaporate, because more particles are at the surface where they can escape.

items.stem: Gallium has a melting point of 30 °C and a boiling point of 2400 °C. What state is it in at 100 °C?
options: it cannot exist at this temperature
items.answer: liquid
items.markingKey: A. B1 liquid: below 30 °C solid, between 30 and 2400 °C liquid, above 2400 °C gas.

items.stem: Mei investigated how the surface area of water affects the rate of evaporation. The method had this weakness: some dishes were placed near a sunny window. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: place all dishes together away from windows and heaters
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: place all dishes together away from windows and heaters

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "evaporation"?
options: A graph of temperature against time as a substance cools
Mass per unit volume of a substance: density = mass ÷ volume
The change from solid to liquid at the melting point
The change from liquid to gas at the surface, at any temperature
items.answer: The change from liquid to gas at the surface, at any temperature
items.markingKey: D. "evaporation" is the change from liquid to gas at the surface, at any temperature.

items.stem: Distinguish between evaporation and boiling.
items.answer: Evaporation happens only at the surface and at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid, with bubbles, at a fixed boiling point.
items.markingKey: Evaporation happens only at the surface and at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid, with bubbles, at a fixed boiling point. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why puddles dry up even when the temperature is below 100 °C.
items.answer: Water evaporates at any temperature: the fastest-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to escape.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Water evaporates at any temperature: the fastest-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to escape. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Leila measured the time taken for 10 cm³ of ethanol to evaporate completely from a dish with a fan at different speeds.

Fan speed setting | Evaporation time / min: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 31.1 | 31.8 | 31.6
2 | 18.3 | 11.8 | 18.3
3 | 13.4 | 13.2 | 13.8
4 | 10.5 | 11.2 | 10.9
5 | 9.1 | 9.7 | 9.6

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean evaporation time at 2, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 11.8 min (trial 2 at 2); mean = 18.30 min
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (11.8) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 18.30 min.

items.stem: Using Freeze-drying coffee and space food as an example, explain sublimation in technology.
items.answer: Food is frozen then put in a vacuum, where the ice sublimes straight to vapour, leaving a light, dry product that keeps for years. NASA used freeze-dried food from the 1960s, and it is now used for coffee, medicines and camping food.
items.markingKey: Context (Food is frozen then put in a vacuum, where the ice sublimes straight to vapour, leaving a light, dry product that keeps for years.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: NASA used freeze-dried food from the 1960s, and it is now used for coffee, medicines and camping food. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to sublimation in technology.

items.stem: Explain, using particles and energy, what happens when an ice cube at −10 °C is heated until it becomes steam at 110 °C.
items.answer: Solid: particles vibrate faster, temperature rises to 0 °C. Melting at 0 °C: energy breaks some forces, temperature constant, particles start to move past each other. Liquid warms to 100 °C: particles move faster. Boiling at 100 °C: energy overcomes remaining forces, particles escape as gas, temperature constant. Gas heats to 110 °C: particles move faster.
items.markingKey: Solid: particles vibrate faster, temperature rises to 0 °C. Melting at 0 °C: energy breaks some forces, temperature constant, particles start to move past each other. Liquid warms to 100 °C: particles move faster. Boiling at 100 °C: energy overcomes remaining forces, particles escape as gas, temperature constant. Gas heats to 110 °C: particles move faster.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "plateau"?
options: The change from liquid to solid at the freezing point
A flat (horizontal) part of a heating or cooling curve where the state is changing
The change from solid directly to gas without becoming a liquid
A state in which particles are close together but arranged randomly and can move past each other
items.answer: A flat (horizontal) part of a heating or cooling curve where the state is changing
items.markingKey: B. "plateau" is a flat (horizontal) part of a heating or cooling curve where the state is changing.

items.stem: A student claims: "The melting point and freezing point of a substance are different temperatures." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: For a pure substance they are the same temperature – it is the temperature at which solid and liquid can exist together.
items.markingKey: For a pure substance they are the same temperature – it is the temperature at which solid and liquid can exist together. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the temperature of a substance stays the same while it freezes, even though it is losing energy to the surroundings.
items.answer: Forces of attraction form between particles as the liquid becomes solid, releasing energy that balances the energy lost. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Forces of attraction form between particles as the liquid becomes solid, releasing energy that balances the energy lost. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: On a heating curve, a liquid’s temperature rises from 44 °C to 84 °C in 8 minutes. Calculate the rate of temperature rise.
items.answer: 5 °C/min

items.stem: Alessia is investigating how the amount of salt dissolved in water affects its freezing point. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If more salt is dissolved, then the freezing point will be lower, because salt particles get in the way of water particles forming the regular arrangement of ice.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If more salt is dissolved, then the freezing point will be lower, because salt particles get in the way of water particles forming the regular arrangement of ice.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "A data logger is always better than a person reading a thermometer for drawing heating curves."
items.answer: Data loggers usually give better data for heating curves, if calibrated and checked.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: takes readings automatically at short intervals; no reading errors. Arguments against: probes must be calibrated; can fail without anyone noticing; students learn less about reading scales. Supported judgement: Data loggers usually give better data for heating curves, if calibrated and checked.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A flat (horizontal) part of a heating or cooling curve where the state is changing"?
items.answer: plateau
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of plateau.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the sloping parts of a heating curve and the flat parts.
items.answer: On sloping parts the energy increases particle speed so temperature rises; on flat parts the energy breaks forces between particles so the state changes at constant temperature.
items.markingKey: On sloping parts the energy increases particle speed so temperature rises; on flat parts the energy breaks forces between particles so the state changes at constant temperature. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "If you keep heating, the temperature always keeps rising." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: During a change of state the temperature stays constant even though energy is still being supplied.
items.markingKey: During a change of state the temperature stays constant even though energy is still being supplied. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Priya recorded the temperature of molten wax as it cooled in a boiling tube (three runs).

Time / min | Temperature / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 92 | 87 | 90
2 | 74 | 75 | 78
4 | 73 | 75 | 76
6 | 51 | 74 | 77
8 | 62 | 62 | 62

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean temperature at 6 min, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 51 °C (trial 1 at 6 min); mean = 75.5 °C
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (51) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 75.5 °C.

items.stem: Describe how to obtain a cooling curve for a sample of stearic acid and explain the shape you would expect.
items.answer: Melt stearic acid in a boiling tube in a hot water bath (about 80 °C); remove, place thermometer/probe in the liquid; record temperature every 30 s for 15 min while it cools; plot temperature against time. Shape: falls quickly, then plateau at about 69 °C as it freezes (forces form, releasing energy), then falls again as the solid cools.
items.markingKey: Melt stearic acid in a boiling tube in a hot water bath (about 80 °C); remove, place thermometer/probe in the liquid; record temperature every 30 s for 15 min while it cools; plot temperature against time. Shape: falls quickly, then plateau at about 69 °C as it freezes (forces form, releasing energy), then falls again as the solid cools.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the amount of salt dissolved in water affects its freezing point. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Dissolve each mass of salt in 50 cm³ water; place 10 cm³ in a boiling tube in a beaker of crushed ice and salt; stir with a thermometer and record temperature every 30 s until solid; plot cooling curves and read the plateau temperature; repeat three times.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (freezing mixtures can cause cold burns – handle with gloves). Model: Dissolve each mass of salt in 50 cm³ water; place 10 cm³ in a boiling tube in a beaker of crushed ice and salt; stir with a thermometer and record temperature every 30 s until solid; plot cooling curves and read the plateau temperature; repeat three times.

items.stem: Which state of a substance usually has the lowest density?
options: All states have the same density
items.answer: Gas
items.markingKey: D. Particles are far apart.

items.stem: Explain the difference between density and mass.
items.answer: Mass is the amount of matter in an object (kg); density is mass per unit volume and depends on the material, not the size of the object.
items.markingKey: Mass is the amount of matter in an object (kg); density is mass per unit volume and depends on the material, not the size of the object. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why an aerosol can must not be heated.
items.answer: Heating makes the gas particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often; the pressure could rise enough to burst the can.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Heating makes the gas particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often; the pressure could rise enough to burst the can. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Mei placed a drop of food colouring in water at different temperatures and timed how long it took to spread evenly through the beaker.

Temperature / °C | Time to spread / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 421 | 420 | 426
20 | 211 | 221 | 208
30 | 145 | 144 | 142
40 | 108 | 109 | 109
50 | 88 | 87 | 85

Calculate the mean time to spread when the temperature was 50 °C.
items.markingKey: M1 (88 + 87 + 85) ÷ 3; A1 86.7 s (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: With reference to Archimedes and the golden crown, explain how it illustrates density and displacement.
items.answer: According to legend, Archimedes compared the water displaced by a crown and by pure gold of the same mass to test if the crown was pure. Displacement is still used to find the volume and density of irregular objects.
items.markingKey: Context (According to legend, Archimedes compared the water displaced by a crown and by pure gold of the same mass to test if the crown was pure.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Displacement is still used to find the volume and density of irregular objects. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to density and displacement.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the concentration of salt water affects its density. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): wipe up spills; salt solution can sting cuts or eyes. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. wipe up spills; salt solution can sting cuts or eyes); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "density".
items.answer: Mass per unit volume of a substance: density = mass ÷ volume
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: mass per unit volume of a substance: density = mass ÷ volume. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Heavy objects sink and light objects float." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Whether an object floats depends on its density compared with the liquid, not its mass – huge steel ships float because their overall density is less than water.
items.markingKey: Whether an object floats depends on its density compared with the liquid, not its mass – huge steel ships float because their overall density is less than water. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the concentration of salt water affects its density, state the dependent variable and describe how Leila should measure it.
items.answer: density of the solution – mass of 50 cm³ measured on a balance ÷ 50
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: density of the solution – mass of 50 cm³ measured on a balance ÷ 50.

items.stem: The density of oak is 0.75 g/cm³. Calculate the mass of a 10 cm³ piece.
items.markingKey: M1 mass = density × volume = 0.75 × 10; A1 7.5 g.

items.stem: Describe how to find the density of an irregular stone and a regular block of wood, and explain how you would decide whether each floats in water.
items.answer: Stone: measure mass on a balance; fill a displacement (eureka) can, lower stone in and collect displaced water in a measuring cylinder = volume; density = mass ÷ volume. Wood: mass on balance; measure length, width, height with a ruler; volume = l × w × h; density = mass ÷ volume. If density < 1.0 g/cm³ it floats; > 1.0 g/cm³ it sinks.
items.markingKey: Stone: measure mass on a balance; fill a displacement (eureka) can, lower stone in and collect displaced water in a measuring cylinder = volume; density = mass ÷ volume. Wood: mass on balance; measure length, width, height with a ruler; volume = l × w × h; density = mass ÷ volume. If density < 1.0 g/cm³ it floats; > 1.0 g/cm³ it sinks.

items.answer: The idea that all matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving

items.stem: Explain why liquids cannot be easily compressed.
items.answer: The particles are already touching, so there is almost no space to push them into.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The particles are already touching, so there is almost no space to push them into. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Steam is invisible water vapour; the white cloud is tiny droplets that have already condensed.

items.answer: Both mass and volume halve, so density stays the same.
items.markingKey: Both mass and volume halve, so density stays the same. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a solid and a liquid.
items.answer: In a solid particles are in fixed, regular positions and vibrate; in a liquid they are still close but random and can move past each other, so it can flow.
items.markingKey: In a solid particles are in fixed, regular positions and vibrate; in a liquid they are still close but random and can move past each other, so it can flow. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: gas
items.markingKey: A. B1 gas: below -218 °C solid, between -218 and -183 °C liquid, above -183 °C gas.

items.stem: On a heating curve, a liquid’s temperature rises from 69 °C to 99 °C in 6 minutes. Calculate the rate of temperature rise.
items.answer: 5 °C/min

items.stem: A piece of iron has a mass of 632 g and a volume of 80 cm³. Calculate its density and state whether it will float or sink in water.
items.answer: 7.9 g/cm³; it will sink
items.markingKey: M1 density = mass ÷ volume = 632 ÷ 80; A1 7.9 g/cm³; B1 sink (water is 1.0 g/cm³).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Scientists should replace the solid–liquid–gas model with a more complicated one in school science."
items.answer: The three-state particle model is a good starting point; its limits should be discussed as students meet substances it cannot explain.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: real substances include plasmas, gels and glasses that do not fit neatly. Arguments against: the simple model explains most everyday observations; more complex models are hard to understand without the basics first. Supported judgement: The three-state particle model is a good starting point; its limits should be discussed as students meet substances it cannot explain.

items.stem: "Using evaporative coolers instead of air conditioning is better in hot countries." Discuss.
items.answer: Evaporative coolers are a good low-energy choice in hot, dry places but not humid ones.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: use much less electricity; cheap to run. Arguments against: only work well in dry air – not in humid climates; use water, which may be scarce. Supported judgement: Evaporative coolers are a good low-energy choice in hot, dry places but not humid ones. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: "A data logger is always better than a person reading a thermometer for drawing heating curves." Discuss.
items.answer: Data loggers usually give better data for heating curves, if calibrated and checked.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: takes readings automatically at short intervals; no reading errors. Arguments against: probes must be calibrated; can fail without anyone noticing; students learn less about reading scales. Supported judgement: Data loggers usually give better data for heating curves, if calibrated and checked. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: "Density tests are a reliable way to detect fake gold coins." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Density is a useful first check, but further tests are needed for sophisticated fakes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: gold is very dense (19.3 g/cm³), most fakes are less dense; quick and non-destructive. Arguments against: tungsten has almost the same density as gold; need accurate measurement of volume. Supported judgement: Density is a useful first check, but further tests are needed for sophisticated fakes. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "solid"?
options: The idea that all matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving
The forces that hold particles together; strongest in solids and weakest in gases
A state in which particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions
Finding the volume of an irregular object by the rise in water level when it is submerged
items.answer: A state in which particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions
items.markingKey: C. "solid" is a state in which particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "melting".
items.answer: The change from solid to liquid at the melting point
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the change from solid to liquid at the melting point. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A pure substance melts at a sharp temperature. What does an impure substance do?
options: Melts over a range of temperatures
Melts at exactly the same temperature
items.answer: Melts over a range of temperatures
items.markingKey: A. Impurities lower and widen the melting point.

items.stem: "Heavy objects sink and light objects float." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Whether an object floats depends on its density compared with the liquid, not its mass – huge steel ships float because their overall density is less than water.
items.markingKey: Whether an object floats depends on its density compared with the liquid, not its mass – huge steel ships float because their overall density is less than water. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a gas and a liquid.
items.answer: In a liquid particles are close together and slide past each other, so it has a fixed volume; in a gas particles are far apart and move freely, so it fills any volume.
items.markingKey: In a liquid particles are close together and slide past each other, so it has a fixed volume; in a gas particles are far apart and move freely, so it fills any volume. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between evaporation and boiling.
items.answer: Evaporation happens only at the surface and at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid, with bubbles, at a fixed boiling point.
items.markingKey: Evaporation happens only at the surface and at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid, with bubbles, at a fixed boiling point. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how a melting point can be used to check the purity of a substance.
items.answer: A pure substance melts at a sharp, known temperature; impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A pure substance melts at a sharp, known temperature; impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why a hot-air balloon rises.
items.answer: Heated air expands so the same mass takes up more volume; it is less dense than the surrounding cooler air.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Heated air expands so the same mass takes up more volume; it is less dense than the surrounding cooler air. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why gases fill any container they are put in.
items.answer: Gas particles move quickly and randomly in all directions with very weak forces between them, so they spread out to fill the space.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Gas particles move quickly and randomly in all directions with very weak forces between them, so they spread out to fill the space. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Jonas measured the time taken for 10 cm³ of ethanol to evaporate completely from a dish with a fan at different speeds.

Fan speed setting | Evaporation time / min: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 34.0 | 35.1 | 35.0
2 | 18.7 | 19.1 | 19.6
3 | 13.9 | 14.6 | 14.6
4 | 12.1 | 11.6 | 11.3
5 | 10.1 | 9.9 | 9.7

Calculate the mean evaporation time when the fan speed setting was 3.
items.markingKey: M1 (13.9 + 14.6 + 14.6) ÷ 3; A1 14.37 min (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem:
Kwame recorded the temperature of molten wax as it cooled in a boiling tube (three runs).

Time / min | Temperature / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 89 | 88 | 86
2 | 70 | 75 | 72
4 | 73 | 70 | 70
6 | 70 | 71 | 69
8 | 59 | 58 | 61

Calculate the percentage change in the mean temperature between 0 min and 8 min.
items.markingKey: M1 means 87.7 and 59.3; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 -32.3% (decrease).

items.stem: Briefly describe Archimedes and the golden crown and explain what it reveals about density and displacement.
items.answer: According to legend, Archimedes compared the water displaced by a crown and by pure gold of the same mass to test if the crown was pure. Displacement is still used to find the volume and density of irregular objects.
items.markingKey: Context (According to legend, Archimedes compared the water displaced by a crown and by pure gold of the same mass to test if the crown was pure.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Displacement is still used to find the volume and density of irregular objects. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to density and displacement.

items.stem: Priya is investigating how the temperature of a gas in a sealed syringe affects its volume. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: temperature of the water bath around the syringe (°C)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: temperature of the water bath around the syringe (°C) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

Sofia measured the time taken for 10 cm³ of ethanol to evaporate completely from a dish with a fan at different speeds.

Fan speed setting | Evaporation time / min: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 37.8 | 38.5 | 38.2

4 | 13.0 | 13.0 | 12.9

Calculate the percentage change in the mean evaporation time between 1 and 5.
items.markingKey: M1 means 38.17 and 11.23; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 -70.6% (decrease).

items.stem: Noah wants to find out how the amount of salt dissolved in water affects its freezing point. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does mass of salt dissolved in 50 cm³ of water affect freezing point?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (mass of salt dissolved in 50 cm³ of water (0, 2, 4, 6, 8 g)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (freezing point read from the plateau of a cooling curve) in a question form.

items.stem: Elena is investigating how the concentration of salt water affects its density. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: mass of salt dissolved in 100 cm³ of water (0, 5, 10, 15, 20 g)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: mass of salt dissolved in 100 cm³ of water (0, 5, 10, 15, 20 g) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the temperature of a gas in a sealed syringe affects its volume. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): take care with hot water; clamp the syringe securely. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. take care with hot water; clamp the syringe securely); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the surface area of water affects the rate of evaporation. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): wipe up spills to avoid slips; handle glass dishes carefully. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. wipe up spills to avoid slips; handle glass dishes carefully); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Amara investigated how the amount of salt dissolved in water affects its freezing point. The method had this weakness: the plateau was hard to see because readings were every 2 min. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: take readings every 15–30 s, or use a temperature probe and data logger
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: take readings every 15–30 s, or use a temperature probe and data logger

items.stem: Diego plans an investigation into how the concentration of salt water affects its density. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (mass of salt dissolved in 100 cm³ of water (0, 5, 10, 15, 20 g)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.
